Eighth grade science · Unit 8.6

Gravity, Orbits & the Solar System

In Unit 11: Earth in Space you used the Sun, Earth, and Moon to explain seasons, phases, and tides. In Unit 8.3 you learned that gravity is a force at a distance. Now we put them together: why do planets orbit, how did the Solar System form, and how do we send spacecraft through it? Use the model-building habits of Unit 0: How Science Works.

Where we left off: Unit 11 explained seasons, phases, and tides, and Unit 8.3 introduced gravity as a field. You may already have learned that the Moon orbits Earth. Here we explain why orbits happen, how the Solar System formed, and how spacecraft use gravity.

Concept 1 · What is an orbit?

An orbit is falling and missing the ground

Gravity pulls a moving object toward the planet, but if it moves sideways fast enough, the ground curves away as fast as it falls. That endless fall is an orbit.

Gravity is the pull that every object with mass has on every other object, and it gets weaker as the distance grows. An orbit is the curved path an object follows as it moves around a much heavier one, like the Moon around Earth or Earth around the Sun. Anything in orbit is moving sideways very fast as well as being pulled inward, so it keeps falling toward the heavy body without ever reaching it. The sideways speed needed is called orbital speed; for a low orbit around Earth it is about 7.7 km/s (4.8 miles per second).

Analogy

Newton's cannonball

Fire a cannon sideways from a tall mountain: the ball lands farther with more speed. Fast enough, and it never lands.

Concept 2 · Kepler's patterns

Farther planets move slower and take longer

Orbits are ellipses. The farther from the Sun, the weaker the gravity, so the slower the speed and the longer the year. Kepler found that (period)² grows as (distance)³.

In the early 1600s Johannes Kepler used careful measurements of the planets to show that each one moves on an ellipse (a stretched circle) with the Sun at one special point, not at the middle. A planet's period is the time it takes to go once around the Sun, which is that planet's year. Distances in the Solar System are huge, so astronomers use the astronomical unit (AU): the average Earth–Sun distance, about 150 million km (93 million miles). The farther a planet is from the Sun, the weaker the pull, the slower it moves, and the longer the path it has to travel.

Analogy

Runners on a track

Outer lanes are longer, so a runner at the same speed needs more time per lap. Planets farther out also move slower, so their years are longer still. Where it breaks: real race lanes are staggered so every runner covers the same distance; planet orbits are not.

Try it

The Solar System from above

Look down on the Solar System from far above the Sun's north pole. All eight planets start lined up. Press play, change the speed, and watch the inner planets lap the outer ones. Pick a planet in the table to follow it. At the slowest speed you can watch the planets spin too.

PlanetDistanceSunlight takesOrbit speedYearYears so farDay (spin)

Distances. One astronomical unit (AU) is the Earth–Sun distance, about 150 million km. Sunlight, the fastest thing there is, needs 8 minutes to reach Earth and about 4 hours to reach Neptune. A car driving 100 km/h without stopping would need about 5,000 years to get to Neptune. The planets are tiny compared with the gaps between them, so no picture can show true size and true distance at once: try “True distances” and notice how the four inner planets crowd close to the Sun.

Spin. Every planet also rotates. Most spin in the same direction they orbit, but Venus spins backward, so slowly that its day (243 Earth days) is longer than its year (225 days). Uranus is tipped on its side (98°). Jupiter, the biggest planet, spins fastest, once in under 10 hours. Watch the “Years so far” column: the farther a planet is, the longer its year, which is Kepler's pattern T² = a³.

Concept 3 · How the Solar System formed

A collapsing cloud made a Sun and disk

About 4.6 billion years ago a cloud of gas and dust collapsed under gravity, spun faster, and flattened into a disk. The Sun formed in the middle; dust clumped into planets. Heat sorted the materials: rock and metal near the Sun, gas and ice farther out.

Astronomers think the Sun and planets formed about 4.6 billion years ago from a nebula, a huge cloud of gas (mostly hydrogen and helium) and dust. When part of the cloud collapsed under its own gravity it spun faster as it shrank, the way a skater spins faster when pulling in their arms, and it flattened into a spinning disk. Most of the material fell to the center and became the Sun; the rest of the disk clumped into planets, moons, asteroids and comets. We can check this story because telescopes photograph young stars in other places that are surrounded by disks right now.

Analogy

Pizza dough

A spinning pizza flattens into a disk. A spinning, collapsing gas cloud flattens too, which is why planets orbit in nearly the same plane.

Concept 4 · Eight worlds

Compare the planets by the numbers

Planets differ in size, gravity, temperature, atmosphere, and year length. Only Earth has liquid surface water and life that we know of.

The eight planets fall into two families. The four terrestrial (rocky) planets, Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars, are small and have solid surfaces. The four giant planets, Jupiter and Saturn (gas giants) and Uranus and Neptune (ice giants), are much bigger and have no solid surface to stand on: Earth is about 12,700 km (7,900 miles) across and Jupiter about 140,000 km (87,000 miles). Surface gravity is how strongly a planet pulls on you where you stand; it depends on the planet's mass and size, not on how far it is from the Sun.

Analogy

Goldilocks planets

Venus is too hot, Mars too cold, Earth is "just right" for liquid water, at least partly because of its distance from the Sun. Where it breaks: distance alone does not decide habitability. Venus is hotter than its distance predicts because of its runaway greenhouse atmosphere, and Mars is cold partly because its air is thin.

Concept 5 · Space technology

Using gravity to explore

Spacecraft use rockets to reach orbit and gravity assists (swinging by planets) to gain speed without fuel. Telescopes, rovers, and probes collect data we cannot get from Earth.

Getting into space means reaching orbital speed, which rockets do by burning fuel. A satellite orbits a planet, a probe travels from world to world, a rover drives on a surface, and a space telescope looks out from above the blurring of Earth's air. To save fuel, probes such as Voyager use a gravity assist: they fly close to a planet and borrow a little of its orbital motion, so its gravity speeds the probe up and bends its path.

Analogy

Slingshot on a merry-go-round

Seen from the Sun, the planet’s motion adds to the probe’s. The planet slows by an amount too tiny to measure; the probe gains speed for free.

Jump onto a spinning merry-go-round and get flung off faster. A probe passing a moving planet steals a bit of its orbital energy.

Check yourself

Can you explain it?

A classmate says astronauts float because there is no gravity in space. Use the idea of orbits to correct them and give the evidence from the ISS data.

Show a model answer

Gravity at the ISS altitude is about 90% of what it is on the ground. The station and astronauts are in free fall, moving sideways at 7.7 km/s, so they keep falling around Earth instead of toward it. Since they all fall together, they feel weightless.

Words to know

orbit
The curved path of an object around another because of gravity.
ellipse
A stretched circle.
period
Time for one orbit.
AU
Astronomical unit: Earth–Sun distance (150 million km).
nebula
A cloud of gas and dust.
terrestrial planet
A rocky inner planet.
gas giant
A large planet of mostly hydrogen and helium.
escape velocity
Speed needed to leave a planet's gravity.
gravity assist
Using a planet's gravity to change a probe's speed.
free fall
Falling with only gravity acting.
Tutor notes: hands-on kit, misconceptions, pacing

Kit (about $10): string and a ball (orbit demo), a stretched lycra sheet or trampoline with marbles (gravity well), a 3 m roll of paper (scale model), clay for planets, a bike wheel or lazy Susan, a flashlight.

  • Concept 1: Swing a ball on a string and let go to see the straight-line path.
  • Concept 2: Roll marbles around a stretched sheet with a heavy ball in the middle.
  • Concept 3: Build a scale model: 1 AU = 10 cm, place the planets.
  • Concept 4: Calculate each planet's year from distance using T² = a³.
  • Concept 5: Make a poster comparing two planets and arguing which is more habitable.

Common misconceptions:

  • "There is no gravity in space." Gravity reaches everywhere.
  • "Orbits are circles." They are ellipses, mostly almost circular.
  • "The Sun is a planet." It is a star.
  • "Planets are in a straight line." They are scattered along their orbits.

Pacing: about five 30-minute sessions. Method link: compare model predictions with data: if T² = a³ predicts Mars's year, check it against the table (Unit 0).
